documents: Liu, Xue, Guo & Zhu (2022), Seismic anisotropy within the subducting northern Philippine Sea plate, SW Japan, using DONET seafloor observation network, Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2021GL096516 (published PDF, 9 pages)
pages_convention: PDF pages counted from 1 (identical to the printed 'n of 9' journal pages)

entry.evidence: It is unclear, however, whether this fossil fabric is preserved or overprinted by the subduction process.

steps.action: The authors pose two open questions. Is the spreading-related fossil fabric of the slab preserved or overprinted during subduction, and how much do slabs contribute to SKS anisotropy?
steps.quote: It is unclear, however, whether this fossil fabric is preserved or overprinted by the subduction process.

steps.action: The authors take from the literature two rival positions on slab anisotropy: a small, ignorable contribution (Long & Becker; Long & Silver) and slab anisotropy dominating SKS (Faccenda et al. 2008).
steps.quote: a recent study proposes that the slab anisotropy is large enough to dominate the SKS anisotropy observed at subduction zones

steps.action: The authors design an observation geometry that isolates the slab: S waves from earthquakes inside the slab, guided along the nPSP and recorded by DONET ocean-bottom seismometers near the trench. This avoids the onshore-station paths that limited Wang & Zhao (2012) and Saiga et al. (2013).
steps.quote: This station-event geometry makes it possible to constrain the seismic anisotropy within the subducted nPSP and to derive its deformation history.

steps.action: The authors select 10 of 20 DONET1 stations by signal-to-noise ratio and 22 intraslab JMA events (25-70 km depth, M2.5-4.0, October 2014 to February 2018) with incidence angles below 35 degrees, and correct the sensor azimuths.
steps.quote: selected 10 stations of high signal to noise ratios out of 20

steps.action: The authors estimate the splitting parameters (fast axis phi, delay time dt) of the S arrivals using the cross-correlation and smallest-eigenvalue-minimization methods.
steps.quote: we applied cross-correlation and the smallest eigenvalue minimization methods on the S wave arrivals

steps.action: The authors keep only measurements on which the two splitting methods agree (|dphi| < 15 degrees, relative ddt < 0.20). Cluster analysis over splitting windows and filter bands chooses an optimum and shows that the result is stable (Figure 2k-l; details in Text S3).
steps.quote: The results are considered stable if the above two methods show a good consistence

steps.action: The authors obtain 29 stable measurements. They trace rays in the 1D JMA2001 model, project them onto a tomographic profile, and group them into ray types I, II and III by path.
steps.quote: We obtained totally 29 stable SWS measurements at 10 stations

steps.action: The authors find that most fast axes are trench-parallel (type I concentrated around N55E, with smaller consistency for types II and III). They compare this with earlier P-wave anisotropy tomography and onshore splitting studies.
steps.quote: most fast axes are parallel or subparallel to the strike of Nankai trough, consistent with the trench-parallel fast axis obtained by P wave anisotropy tomography

steps.action: The authors observe that delay time increases linearly with event depth, except for type II. They read this as longer ray paths in a uniformly anisotropic slab (Figure 3c).
steps.quote: showing a linear increasing trend with event depths

steps.action: The authors check the premise that rays travel mainly along the slab. Type I and II waveforms show longer coda than records at onshore stations (Figure S1), consistent with waveguide scattering. They argue that the waveguide does not bias splitting because only the first cycles are used.
steps.quote: The seismic waveforms of type I and II show longer coda compared with the stations on land

steps.action: The authors compute what the rival 'continental crust contributes' predicts, using a two-layer anisotropy model built from their own and published splitting parameters (Figure S2). The observed fast axis matches the lower layer, and the modeled times are consistent with the observed times to some extent.
steps.quote: we have performed a two-layer anisotropy modeling based on the SWS parameters obtained in this study as well as in previous studies

steps.action: The authors exclude a significant crustal contribution and attribute the splitting mainly to the subducted nPSP, supported by the delay-depth trend. They state that they cannot separate slab mantle from slab crust.
steps.quote: the contribution from the continental crust is insignificant

steps.action: The authors state two rival origins of the anisotropy: olivine lattice preferred orientation (LPO) from seafloor spreading, which predicts a fast axis parallel to the paleo-spreading direction and the trough, and trench-parallel serpentinized hydrated faults.
steps.quote: Another origin of slab anisotropy is associated with the serpentinized hydrated faults

steps.action: The authors compare the observed fast axis with both origins. Both predict a trench-parallel fast axis, so the observation cannot single out the leading source.
steps.quote: we could not distinguish which anisotropy source plays a leading role in the observed nPSP anisotropy

steps.action: The authors estimate anisotropy strength from the delay times with the Hirose (2008) velocity model, assuming constant anisotropy along each ray: 2-3% for type I and 1-2% for types II and III.
steps.quote: the anisotropy strength estimated for is 2%–3% for type I and 1%–2% for both type II and III seismic rays

steps.action: The authors compare the strength with the subducting PSP beneath northern Taiwan, the Nazca slab, and the average upper mantle; the nPSP is weaker than all three.
steps.quote: our inferred 2%–3% anisotropy strength of nPSP is relatively weaker than the subducting PSP at northern Taiwan and Nazca plate

steps.action: The authors reject, for Nankai, the rival that slab anisotropy dominates SKS splitting: type I slab delays of 0.37-0.48 s are too small for the observed 0.70-1.5 s SKS delays.
steps.quote: the splitting times of 0.37–0.48 s for type I seismic rays are not able to dominate the observed 0.70–1.5 s SKS splitting times in Japan

steps.action: The authors attribute the scattered fast axes and smaller delays of type II and III to contamination by structures outside the slab (overriding sediments and crust, sub-slab mantle, oceanic crust, accretionary prism). This is an auxiliary explanation, not a revision of the slab-anisotropy claim.
steps.quote: suggesting the obtained slab anisotropy of nPSP may be contaminated by structures outside nPSP

steps.action: The authors use published thermal models showing the seismogenic nPSP is below the 900 C threshold for overprinting olivine fabric.
steps.quote: Thermal modeling results show that the subducted nPSP with seismicity has a temperature lower than 900°C

steps.action: The authors contrast the nPSP with the older Nazca slab, whose fossil fabric at 200-400 km depth was overprinted by internal deformation during subduction.
steps.quote: This is different with the over 45 Ma Nazca slab

steps.action: The authors keep the claim that the spreading-related fossil fabric of the 20-30 Ma nPSP is preserved during subduction, possibly strengthened by serpentinized faults, with 1-3% anisotropy.
steps.quote: the anisotropy within the fossilized fabric of the 20–30 Ma nPSP may be preserved in general and was not modified during the [...]

tree.answer: Seismic anisotropy inside the subducting nPSP slab
No; inferred from shear-wave splitting of slab-guided S waves
Measure the slab anisotropy and judge whether the fossil fabric is preserved
Location (slab vs overriding crust); origin (olivine LPO vs serpentinized faults); slab dominance of SKS vs small contribution
Yes for location (two-layer model, delay-depth trend) and SKS dominance; no for origin (both predict trench-parallel)
Found: natural intraslab earthquakes recorded by an existing seafloor network

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: 22 events and 29 measurements in three ray groups; delay grows with depth
Two splitting methods agree; stable across windows and filter bands; coda check against onshore stations
Fossil fabric likely preserved; best explanation, with the origin left undistinguished

end.claim: The subducting nPSP has a sub-trench-parallel fast axis with 1-3% anisotropy, best explained as a spreading-related fossil fabric preserved during subduction (possibly strengthened by trench-parallel serpentinized faults) and too weak to dominate Nankai SKS splitting.

decisive_move.sentence: Choosing intraslab events recorded by DONET ocean-bottom seismometers near the trench, so that rays travel a long distance inside the slab, is what lets slab anisotropy be separated from the overriding plate and mantle wedge; without this geometry there is no slab-specific measurement.

gates.evidence: Action: the question of isolating slab anisotropy directed the choice of intraslab events and offshore stations (p. 2), but no specific hypothesis did. Claim: the in-slab location faced a test it could have failed (two-layer modeling and the delay-depth trend, pp. 5-6), and SKS dominance was tested against observed SKS delays (p. 7). The preservation claim rests on consistency with the spreading direction and on cited thermal models, and the origin rivals were not distinguished (pp. 6-7). Registration: nothing is stated as fixed before the data were examined; the stability criteria appear in Methods with no statement of when they were set.

imports.item: Cluster analysis (Calinski & Harabasz 1974; Duda & Hart 1973) to choose the optimum splitting window and frequency band

limits: Only the main paper was supplied; Supporting Information (Texts S1-S3, Tables S1-S3, Figures S1-S2) was not seen, so the cluster-analysis details, the per-measurement table and the two-layer modeling result were coded from main-text statements. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence was coded. Sub-claim statuses: the type I fast axis (about N55E, average uncertainty 9.6 degrees) is estimate_with_resolution; the anisotropy strength (1-3%) is estimate_with_resolution but rests on an assumed constant anisotropy along each ray and a chosen velocity model, without a formal uncertainty; the location of anisotropy in the slab rather than the continental crust is best_explanation; slab mantle versus slab crust is no_conclusion; LPO versus serpentinized faults as the leading source is no_conclusion. The abstract and conclusions say the fabric is 'strengthened by' the faults, while the discussion says the two sources cannot be distinguished (inference: the headline framing is stronger than the discussion). Preservation is inferred from consistency with the paleo-spreading direction plus cited thermal models; no test of overprinting was run here. Ray paths use a 1D model with no 3D propagation effects. The Data Availability statement names Hi-net, not DONET, as the data source; the access route for the DONET data is unclear. The paper makes no explicit 'first' or 'previously unknown' statement; novelty is implied only by the claim that the station-event geometry isolates the slab (p. 2).

disagreements.target: Wang and Zhao (2012), P-wave anisotropy tomography
disagreements.support: The authors argue the tomographic anisotropy at slab depths cannot exclude contributions from outside the slab, then confirm its trench-parallel direction with slab-guided splitting.
disagreements.quote: the resulting anisotropy at the slab depths cannot rule out the contributions from structures outside the slab

disagreements.target: Saiga et al. (2013), onshore SWS of intraslab events
disagreements.support: The onshore rays travelled only briefly in the slab and were affected by the overriding plate and mantle wedge; the authors use offshore stations with long in-slab paths instead.
disagreements.quote: these seismic rays traveled only a short distance within the slab and the SWS results are significantly influenced by the overriding plate

disagreements.target: Faccenda et al. (2008), slab anisotropy large enough to dominate SKS anisotropy at subduction zones
disagreements.support: Type I slab delays of 0.37-0.48 s are too small to account for the 0.70-1.5 s SKS delays observed in Japan, so the proposal does not hold at Nankai.
disagreements.quote: The relatively weak anisotropy of subducted nPSP is not be able to dominate the observed SKS anisotropy at the Nankai subduction zone.
